rootCause.summary:
preindex_budget derives max_entries from the last byte signature resembling an EOCD, without validating that candidate's disk/comment/directory fields. The ZIP reader uses validated candidate selection and retries earlier EOCDs when the last one fails. A false zero-count footer in the real comment therefore passes preindex while ZipArchive indexes the earlier real directory. Neither admit nor read_package caps the actual opened archive length, and the collapsed-duplicate comparison also uses the unrelated false count.
The assigned source supplies an alternative invalid-candidate framing: an offset at/past the false EOCD makes zip reject that candidate. Both framings use the same last-signature/validated-selection mismatch. A post-open length check bounds later processing but cannot undo metadata already allocated while indexing.
A separate, incomplete EOCD/ZIP64 parser is treated as authoritative for resource admission even though the delegated ZIP parser chooses its own footer/count semantics. Indexed entries are not reconciled to the active limit.

finding.summary: The preindex guard checks an independently parsed EOCD total-entry count, while zip9.0.5 uses the ZIP32 per-disk count to construct its index. findings.title: Untrusted Markdown reference documents reach unchecked recursive XML parsing
findings.summary: Markdown conversion opens a caller-supplied reference DOCX using byte-only package bounds and parses its main XML without the XML-depth admission gate. severity.changeConditions: Enforcing the missing input/derived-work boundary removes this path; isolated workers reduce shared-service impact.

rootCause.summary:
DocxOptions.reference is copied into a template and opened by PartFs, which enforces ZIP budgets but does not admit ordinary document XML. assemble reads the selected main part and passes it to frame/final_section. final_section calls the trusted-only parse_xdocument on those bytes, reaching unguarded recursive parse_element. Native/Python/WASM wrappers forward reference bytes without adding that missing XML gate; native CLI read_document only sniffs the container.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: The reference-template path treats PartFs::open's ZIP/inflation bounds as sufficient and invokes Dom::parse_xdocument on unchecked reference XML, contrary to that API's requirement for prior XML policy enforcement.

findings.remediation: Admit every supplied reference DOCX under explicit active InputLimits before metadata, style, scholar, frame or other reference XML consumers parse it, or consistently use checked parsing at every main and preserved auxiliary XML boundary. Propagate limits and typed refusals across Rust/Python/WASM/CLI paths.

returnedFinding.title: Markdown reference documents reach recursive XML parsing without depth admission
returnedFinding.body: A caller-supplied reference DOCX is opened with PartFs::open and its main XML is passed into frame/final_section without package admission or checked XML parsing. PartFs bounds ZIP sizes and entry counts but does not enforce XML depth on document parts. final_section calls the explicitly unchecked Dom::parse_xdocument, whose parse_element recursively descends for every nested element without a depth limit. Consequently, a deeply nested reference document can exhaust the native Python/Rust process stack or trap the WASM instance despite the advertised max_xml_depth=256 policy. This is reachable through Rust markdown_to_docx, Python from_markdown(reference=...), WASM markdownToDocx(..., reference), and CLI --reference-doc conversion paths.
returnedFinding.attackerControl: Reference DOCX bytes supplied to an application or conversion workflow accepting untrusted templates.
returnedFinding.protectedAsset: Availability of the embedding Python/Rust process, conversion worker or WASM instance.
prerequisites: The application accepts an attacker-supplied reference document rather than selecting exclusively trusted templates.
The application does not independently admit/check the reference before conversion.

findings.title: Large page coordinates make border rendering loop without progress
findings.summary: Finite page dimensions and margins from DOCX can place a dotted border at coordinates where its f32 increment rounds to zero. Rendering then loops indefinitely while appending drawing operations, exhausting memory.

severity.rationale: Ordinary document rendering crosses from supplier-controlled section geometry to a nonterminating loop; availability is affected without host configuration. CPU/memory limits contain the worker but still permit denial of service.
severity.changeConditions: Reject excessive geometry, compute bounded integer segment counts and enforce operation budgets; isolation reduces shared-host consequences.

confidence.rationale: Parent confirmed unbounded geometry, text-relative endpoints, f32 step and per-iteration push. At1e9 float spacing exceeds1, proving nonprogress. No runtime hang executed.

codeEvidence.label: Page and margins accept unbounded lengths
codeEvidence.explanation: Attacker page width and left margin become f32 coordinates without a maximum.

codeEvidence.label: Border widths and style determine the step
codeEvidence.explanation: sz=1 maps to 0.24pt; dotted style later clamps on/off to0.5 each.

codeEvidence.label: Text-relative border uses large margins
codeEvidence.explanation: Default text-relative border places left endpoint at the unbounded margin.

codeEvidence.label: Float loop lacks progress and operation budget
codeEvidence.explanation: At p=1e9, f32 p+1 equals p; condition remains true and each iteration adds an operation.

codeEvidence.label: Each iteration appends a drawing operation
codeEvidence.explanation: Even zero-length coordinate progress pushes a minimum-width FillRect, exhausting memory.

rootCause.summary: `apply_sect_pr()` accepts unbounded f32 page dimensions and margins. A text-relative border starts at that margin. Dotted-border painting clamps on/off intervals to0.5 each, then repeatedly adds1 to the f32 position. At a large finite coordinate this addition cannot change the value; the while condition remains true and each iteration pushes another FillRect.

findings.remediation: Validate finite, reasonable page/margin/border geometry before layout. Use a bounded integer segment count instead of open-ended float accumulation, enforce a maximum border-operation budget, and explicitly refuse any step that cannot advance.

counterEvidence: All trigger numbers are finite; a NaN/infinity-only check would not fix the problem.
word_pgsz_pt only adjusts two A4 sizes and otherwise returns the supplied size.
MAX_PAGE_PIXELS applies after this layout loop, and PDF/render reports reach it too.
Process limits can kill the worker, not make the loop terminate.
limitations: No product execution, hang or allocation-failure reproduction performed.

findings.title: Redaction succeeds while UTF-16 XML retains the removed text
findings.summary: The redact operation can return successful clean and redline documents while a supported BOM-marked UTF-16LE/BE auxiliary XML part still contains the same confidential text. Its XML leak branch uses lossy UTF-8 and misses the retained copy, which a recipient can recover after sharing.

severity.rationale: An outgoing document can disclose text the user explicitly asked to remove. A supplier can place a duplicate in supported customXml and the user performs ordinary redaction; successful checking makes the confidentiality failure likely when that document is shared.
severity.changeConditions: Impact depends on sensitivity and subsequent sharing. Consistent BOM-aware decoding and fail-closed scanning remove the bypass.

confidence.rationale: Parent verified UTF16 admission, raw part retention/output, XML-only lossy UTF8 branch and success gate. Baseline validation allows unchanged auxiliary issues. No product execution was performed.

codeEvidence.label: UTF-16 XML copies survive redaction without triggering the leak gate
codeEvidence.explanation: A supported UTF-16 custom XML part passes admission's BOM-aware decoder and remains raw in PartFs. leaks branches by XML filename suffix and invokes UTF-8-lossy parsing rather than the admission decoder. rootCause.summary: Admission deliberately transcodes BOM-marked UTF16 XML for validation, but PartFs preserves its raw bytes. After visible body redaction, `leaks_within()` routes every .xml/.rels part into `String::from_utf8_lossy()` and semantic scanning. Its UTF16 byte search exists only for non-XML parts. Thus NUL-interleaved UTF16 copies are invisible; `check_redactions()` sees no hits and permits output with those unchanged bytes. The standalone leaks API and both prepared artifacts use this same branch; ordinary Transitional input does not require Strict normalization to rewrite the untouched auxiliary part.

findings.remediation: Decode every XML part with the same BOM-aware policy as admission before semantic leak scanning. Fail closed on unsupported/undecodable representations and retain raw UTF8 and both UTF16 byte-order checks as defense in depth. Use the same decoding across leak checks and package validation.

rootCause.summary:
`scrub()` invokes `scrub_properties()` when docprops is selected. That routine resolves only docProps/core.xml, docProps/app.xml and docProps/custom.xml constants, rather than actual property relationship targets. If custom properties use another part name, even relationship cleanup is skipped. PartFs preserves arbitrary ordinary parts and their relationships; output serialization retains untouched metadata. Validation compares newly introduced issues rather than the requested privacy postcondition. The assigned trace additionally follows public README sharing guidance, authoritative package-level relationships and preservation of every surviving output part. Admission and structural validation do not mandate conventional metadata filenames or enforce anonymization.
Privacy sanitization selects conventional filenames instead of all relationship/content-type-selected property parts and does not verify requested removal postconditions.

Preserve intentional title/subject/application and revision-date retention. Missing/invalid selected targets require explicit refusal or documented safe handling; default public and CLI callers must enforce the same postcondition.

findings.title: Opaque DTD and top-level CDATA bypass package XML depth checks
findings.summary:
Package admission ignores opaque DTD and top-level CDATA events, while the permissive DOM handles top-level <! constructs by skipping only to the first '>'. A delimiter within a quoted entity or CDATA body exposes deeply nested literal markup as recursive elements, bypassing admission depth and potentially exhausting the host stack. Rendering and lazy WmlDocument main-part access are preserved affected entrypoints.
An internal-subset comment with a literal > supplies an additional hidden-tag framing at the same declaration boundary.

severity.rationale: A small ordinary-named document part can cause process stack exhaustion through public document processing. Impact is availability without privileged configuration; no external entity fetch or code execution is asserted.
severity.changeConditions: Rejecting DTD declarations at package admission and enforcing parser depth makes the representations agree. Isolated workers reduce shared-host impact.

confidence.rationale: Independent parent traced both parser interpretations and checked the locked quick-xml0.42 DTD parser's quote-sensitive skip. No runtime stack exhaustion was executed; the exact crash depth depends on runtime stack size.

rootCause.summary:
`check_xml_depth()` counts Start/Empty events and ignores DocType. The streaming reader correctly consumes the complete internal subset, including quoted element-like text. `parse_document()` instead skips any declaration only to the first closing angle bracket, even inside that literal, then treats the remaining literal markup as actual elements. Its recursive element parser has no independent depth guard. The checked XML API's explicit DTD rejection is absent from package admission. WmlDocument::from_bytes admits/stores parts and main_document later parses the same main bytes unchecked. A single quoted internal entity value with nested literal tags is sufficient; the earlier two-entity illustration is not a prerequisite.
The package gate and permissive DOM disagree on lexical boundaries of DTD/top-level CDATA. Admission ignores opaque tokens while the DOM's first-> skip reinterprets their remaining bytes as recursively nested markup.
The additional legal internal-subset-comment framing uses a literal > before nested-looking tags, exposing comment content through the same first-delimiter skip; it needs no entity expansion.
The rendering corroboration also retains quoted ENTITY/ATTLIST internal-subset handling in quick-xml 0.42 (parser/dtd.rs:28-60,122-144,196-205; reader/state.rs:163-173). A Transitional main part without altChunk or strict namespace rewriting remains unchanged before unchecked with_layout parsing; main-part existence/content-type checks are not declaration safety checks.

findings.remediation: Align admission and DOM lexical/structural semantics for every opaque <! construct. Reject unsupported DTD and CDATA/text outside the root consistently with checked XML validation, and enforce active depth during DOM construction or use the checked API before every untrusted consumer. If opaque constructs are supported, consume their complete grammar rather than the first '>'. A DTD-only refusal does not fix the top-level CDATA subcase; retain valid in-root CDATA.

validation.summary:
A valid internal entity declaration can contain a long literal with nested tag text without using the entity. quick-xml0.42 consumes the entire declaration as DocType (cached src/parser/dtd.rs:28-59,194-200,262-265), so package depth remains shallow. The DOM skip ends at the literal's first tag terminator and immediately enters recursion over the remaining literal. Normal rendering parses before it can reject the phantom root. This is independent of non-XML filenames.
Verified current quick-xml 0.42.0 parser/dtd.rs:28-30,124-135,194-199 preserves quoted entity values while scanning the internal subset, and reader/state.rs:163-173 emits the entire declaration as DocType. Admission ignores that event. The raw parser uses its first-'>' search regardless of quotation and resumes element parsing, so sufficiently deep literal tags can exceed the admitted depth.
Parent verified admission event match, DOM top-level skip and recursion plus WmlDocument admission/lazy parse. Current direct dependency quick-xml0.42.0 (Cargo.toml) treats quoted ENTITY content as one DTD and emits one DocType; local parser/dtd.rs:194-202,262-265 and reader/state.rs:163-174 confirm it. A quoted literal containing many opening/closing tags can remain below physical byte budgets but exceed DOM stack depth. Top-level CDATA is a sibling opaque-token path.

Installed quick-xml 0.42 source parser/dtd.rs:28-60,122-144,196-205 and reader/state.rs:163-173 show that quoted ENTITY/ATTLIST content is returned within one DocType event. Main-part metadata checks inspect existence/content type rather than XML declaration safety. with_layout then parses the unchanged Transitional main XML.
Assigned discovery-0010 Standard corroboration (source validation, not reducer verification): Parent read admission's event match, installed quick-xml0.42 quote-sensitive DTD state, WmlDocument constructor/main parse, and DOM declaration/recursive branches. A quoted replacement beginning with > then nested markup is not counted as elements by admission but is consumed by DOM recursion. Checked raw-XML validation rejects DTDs and is not the affected entry.

rootCause.summary:
`check_xml_depth()` counts Start/Empty events and ignores DocType. The streaming reader correctly consumes the complete internal subset, including quoted element-like text. `parse_document()` instead skips any declaration only to the first closing angle bracket, even inside that literal, then treats the remaining literal markup as actual elements. Its recursive element parser has no independent depth guard. The checked XML API's explicit DTD rejection is absent from package admission. WmlDocument::from_bytes admits/stores parts and main_document later parses the same main bytes unchecked. A single quoted internal entity value with nested literal tags is sufficient; the earlier two-entity illustration is not a prerequisite.
The package gate and permissive DOM disagree on lexical boundaries of DTD/top-level CDATA. Admission ignores opaque tokens while the DOM's first-> skip reinterprets their remaining bytes as recursively nested markup.
The additional legal internal-subset-comment framing uses a literal > before nested-looking tags, exposing comment content through the same first-delimiter skip; it needs no entity expansion.
The rendering corroboration also retains quoted ENTITY/ATTLIST internal-subset handling in quick-xml 0.42 (parser/dtd.rs:28-60,122-144,196-205; reader/state.rs:163-173). A Transitional main part without altChunk or strict namespace rewriting remains unchanged before unchecked with_layout parsing; main-part existence/content-type checks are not declaration safety checks.

Reject unsupported DTD and CDATA/text outside the root consistently with checked XML validation, and enforce active depth during DOM construction or use the checked API before every untrusted consumer. If opaque constructs are supported, consume their complete grammar rather than the first '>'. A DTD-only refusal does not fix the top-level CDATA subcase; retain valid in-root CDATA.

findings.title: npm plan recording follows a predictable staging symlink
findings.summary: When recording plan operations, the npm CLI writes to a basename/PID staging path without exclusive creation. A local attacker who can create entries in that directory can redirect the write to an unrelated file writable by the CLI user.

severity.rationale: This is a local, conditional file-integrity failure: exploitation needs attacker write access to the plan directory and prediction/observation of the CLI PID. The target must be writable by the victim. These constrained prerequisites lower likelihood.
severity.changeConditions: A workflow routinely recording plans in a directory writable by less-trusted users increases likelihood. An exclusive regular staging file in a private unpredictable directory removes the link-following path.

confidence.rationale: Source directly constructs predictable partial name, calls default fs.writeFileSync and only then renames. No exclusive/no-follow protection applies; no runtime filesystem manipulation was performed.

codeEvidence.label: Plan recording route
codeEvidence.explanation: A normal edit with plan plus operation flags enters recordPlan.

codeEvidence.label: Predictable staging path is followed by default write
codeEvidence.explanation: Directory attacker can plant the basename/PID partial as symlink; writeFileSync follows it and truncates referent before rename.

rootCause.summary: `runEdit()` routes plan-plus-operation flags to `recordPlan()`. It derives the temporary pathname solely from target basename and process PID and calls `fs.writeFileSync()` with default truncating write semantics. A preexisting symlink at that pathname is followed, modifying its referent before `renameSync()` can publish the plan. Resolving the intended plan target does not validate the separate staging entry.

findings.remediation: Create an unpredictable private staging directory next to the plan and open the staged regular file exclusively. Write through its held descriptor and rename only that file. At minimum refuse every preexisting staging entry using exclusive creation rather than default truncating writes.

counterEvidence: Requires local shared-directory write and a predictable PID; no extra OS file permissions are obtained.
Intentional symlink resolution for the operator-selected plan is separate from the attacker-selected staging link.
Native Rust publication uses private UUID staging/exclusive creation but the npm path does not call it.
Dry-run skips the write.
limitations: No symlink creation or product execution was performed.
No actual shared-directory deployment was supplied; this prerequisite remains conditional.
validation.summary: No filesystem check or exclusive open lies between partial-name construction and writeFileSync. Precreation of that name can select a different victim-writable file outside the plan directory. Subsequent rename moves the staging link, after the referent has already been overwritten.

dataflow.outcome: Unrelated victim-writable file overwritten with plan JSON.

findings.title: Repeated HTML chunk references bypass conversion memory budgets
findings.summary: A DOCX can repeatedly reference one modest HTML part. The renderer admits the small original package, then copies and converts that chunk separately for every reference and concatenates all generated XML. The resulting allocation and work can exceed package budgets by orders of magnitude. For example, 10,000 short references to one 1 MiB ordinary HTML paragraph can imply roughly 10 GiB of generated XML; this is a static estimate, not a runtime measurement.

severity.rationale: An untrusted document supplier can choose many tiny references and one ordinary HTML part that fit original byte/depth/entry limits. The direct outcome is memory/CPU exhaustion in the embedding process or WASM instance. No service deployment is assumed; process isolation limits collateral impact.
severity.changeConditions: Shared unsandboxed upload processing increases impact; a cumulative expanded-byte/node budget enforced before append removes this path.

confidence.rationale: Parent inspected admission order, relationship load, raw HTML acceptance, per-reference conversion and unlimited output append; no runtime reproduction.

rootCause.summary:
`with_layout` admits only the original ZIP. `altchunk::expand` treats each reference independently, reloads the same bytes, rebuilds its HTML as WML and appends the result to one String, without a reference/output budget. The package's original bytes and entries therefore do not bound its expanded representation.
Each internal chunk occurrence adds its full converted content without cumulative import accounting. The original package-size budget applies to stored parts once, not their potentially multiplicative logical reuse.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): Resource admission charges each physical package part once, but the embedded-content transformation can repeatedly materialize that part without charging generated bytes or structural work.

findings.remediation: Make altChunk expansion fallible under active cumulative expanded-byte, node/element, depth, work and occurrence budgets. Check contributions before conversion/allocation/append, including repeated internal relationships and MIME-decoded chunks, and validate generated XML under active limits before DOM construction. Caching may reduce repeated conversion CPU but cannot replace the total-output budget.

findings.title: Python CLI output/plan and npm direct-output symlinks can overwrite unrelated files
findings.summary: Python and npm ordinary-output helpers check pathname existence separately from truncating writes; a local writer of the selected directory can replace an output name and redirect generated bytes to a victim-writable file. Python plan recording additionally uses a predictable basename/PID partial pathname without exclusive creation. The assigned report also corroborates npm plan staging, which is represented by the separately retained symlink-following.plan-staging finding. Without --force, a stable symlink to an existing referent is refused; post-preflight substitution bypasses that refusal, and a dangling link can pass the existence test. Filesystem/OS protections and shared-directory authority remain prerequisites.

severity.rationale: Medium integrity impact with medium likelihood: this is a local shared-directory attack requiring victim CLI execution in an attacker-writable directory, plus successful name replacement or prediction/observation of the PID-based staging name. No remote exposure or privileged execution is established.
severity.changeConditions: Higher impact requires a victim with greater filesystem privileges and an exploitable writable target; private non-writable output directories remove the attacker prerequisite.

confidence.rationale: Source directly shows nonexclusive, symlink-following writes after preflight and predictable plan staging in both adapters; platform behavior was assessed statically, with no exploit executed.

Python/npm direct-output authorization is a non-atomic exists check followed by a symlink-following truncating write. Python plan recording separately derives a predictable PID partial and opens it without exclusive/no-follow semantics. findings.summary: Distinct font-table aliases may all reference one embedded font part. Rendering eagerly loads every alias, copies the full font and retains a separate buffer for each name, multiplying a small admitted package into gigabytes of memory even if its body never uses those fonts.

rootCause.summary:
`parse_font_table_xml()` stores attacker-selected distinct names and embedded relationship IDs. After physical package admission, `with_layout()` calls `load_embedded_fonts()` for every table row. Each unknown alias resolves the same part, calls `deobfuscate_odttf()` which immediately copies all bytes, then stores a new allocation keyed by alias/style. No resolved-part cache or aggregate decoded-font budget shares or bounds repeated copies.
Fonts::for_document subsequently visits every retained alias; its later u16 face-index conversion does not prevent already retained per-alias payload copies.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): A physical resource charged once by package admission is decoded and cloned into independent Arc allocations per attacker-chosen family/style alias without aggregate accounting.

findings.remediation:
Cache decoded font buffers by resolved package part and effective obfuscation key, share Arc values across aliases, and enforce an aggregate decoded-font allocation/work budget before copying.
Enforce face-count limits before decoding/retention and load only used faces where possible; cover all four style slots and different effective keys.

counterEvidence: Known catalogue families are skipped; use distinct unknown names.
Invalid fonts are skipped; a single valid embedded font is sufficient.
The map stores Arc values, but each iteration creates new data and a fresh Arc; there is no source-part sharing here.
ZIP byte and XML depth/attribute limits do not charge multiplicity of font aliases.
Catalogue family names are skipped, but attackers can choose rare names.
Invalid fonts are rejected, but a single valid font can be reused.
Arc values do not deduplicate separate Vec allocations.
The later u16 face-index cap occurs after font bytes have already been cloned and retained.
Fixed catalogue families skipped, but arbitrary distinct names are accepted.
Face validity rejects malformed fonts; one valid reused font satisfies it.
Arc ownership shares only each newly cloned allocation, not copies across aliases.
Conversion-scoped lifetime prevents persistent leak but not in-call exhaustion.
Archive byte limits and recommended process memory limits do not remove alias amplification.

codeEvidence.label: Numeric custom XML identifiers bypass the final redaction check
codeEvidence.explanation: xml_holds checks attribute values but suppresses any matching numeric/hex value when the attribute's local name appears in a broad structural-name list. It never checks namespace, owning element or package part. Custom XML business data such as metadata id='12345678' inherits an exemption intended for OOXML layout numbers, so final output checking overlooks a remaining secret.

rootCause.summary: `check_redactions()` refuses outputs only when `scrub::leaks()` finds the target. For XML attributes, `xml_holds()` ignores a matching value if its local name appears in `NUMERIC_ATTRIBUTES` and its value is hexadecimal-looking. The exemption checks neither namespace nor owning element/part. Thus business XML `<customer id="123456789"/>`, including a business-namespaced `id`, is treated like an OOXML layout identifier. Ordinary body redaction leaves that auxiliary part unchanged and the final scan reports no residual target.

findings.remediation: Remove numeric exemptions from strict redaction verification, or restrict them to verified OOXML namespace/element/attribute combinations representing exclusively generated layout state. Always scan arbitrary custom XML business attributes.

counterEvidence: Exempting genuine OOXML dimensions/generated IDs avoids unrelated short numeric matches and is covered by existing tests.
That purpose does not establish arbitrary custom XML business identifiers as safe; the code does not constrain namespace/element/part.
Nonnumeric attribute values are scanned normally.
Scanner iterates every ZIP entry and fails closed on archive/read/name/budget errors.
UTF8 XML text/comments/PI/ordinary textual attributes and split Word runs are scanned.
Numeric OOXML layout attributes have intentional false-positive exemptions; arbitrary custom data has no such structural guarantee.
limitations: No dynamic integration reproduction; disclosure additionally requires sharing the returned DOCX.
No application/test execution or constructed package.
Finding establishes clean-output preservation; it does not require every comparer path to preserve all auxiliary data identically.
validation.method: Preserved already-validated Standard evidence and attack paths; serial semantic remediation-subsumption reduction only, without code inspection, new validation, execution or attack-path analysis
validation.summary:
A custom XML attribute with `id=123456789` reaches the matching-value branch, passes `is_number()`, and is skipped solely because local_name is id. No other text node need contain the identifier after body redaction. The retained custom part is serialized verbatim; the check then permits the result.
Assigned discovery-0007 corroboration (preserved Standard static validation; no reducer verification): Independently verified NUMERIC_ATTRIBUTES484-519 includes id/num/x/before; is_number522-524 accepts all ASCII hex digits; xml_holds543-550 applies the exemption to every XML element. Arbitrary retained customXml id values are not structurally restricted, and untouched custom data persists into clean output. Existing tests625-631 intentionally permit real OOXML sizes but do not constrain exemptions to that schema.

rootCause.summary: Admission explicitly transcodes UTF-16LE/BE with a BOM, so bounded valid property XML is accepted. The metadata scrubber's `Part::load()` instead calls `part_string()`, which interprets original bytes as UTF-8 lossily. A UTF-16 BOM becomes replacement characters, not the Unicode BOM stripped by `parse_xdocument()`. The permissive parser stops before creating a root; `Part::load()` returns `None` and `scrub_properties()` silently skips the core/app fields. Unchanged raw bytes serialize back out, while the final general-validation comparison rejects only increased findings rather than failed privacy removal.

findings.remediation: Use a shared encoding-aware XML decoder for selected metadata parts, and fail closed when a selected part cannot be parsed or requested identifying values remain. Handle both UTF-16 endiannesses consistently with admission.

findings.title: Tiny Markdown table metadata can trigger unbounded cell allocation
findings.summary: A caller-controlled cells paragraph range is converted into an unbounded count and used to append padding cells. A tiny Markdown table with a range such as p0-p1000000000 causes roughly a billion padding entries to be allocated before DOCX assembly, exhausting CPU and memory in Rust, Python, or WASM conversion hosts. The new corroboration explicitly matches two metadata ranges to a header and data row without breaks; MOST_GRID=64 and arithmetic overflow checks do not bound these valid row counts.

severity.rationale: A small untrusted Markdown input can exhaust or terminate its processing host. Reachability is direct through public byte/string APIs; remote or multi-user service exposure is conditional, and there is no confidentiality or integrity compromise.
severity.changeConditions: Process memory/CPU limits and worker isolation constrain impact; a shared remotely exposed conversion service would increase operational impact.

confidence.rationale: Static source tracing establishes the unchecked numeric count, default public conversion path, and count-driven Vec growth; runtime exhaustion was deliberately not executed.

findings.title: Unbounded document table spans exhaust memory during rendering
findings.summary: Untrusted direct OOXML gridSpan/gridBefore/gridAfter and imported HTML/MHT colspan values become unrestricted output column counts. Tiny metadata can request a billion columns, driving dense column/preference/merge vectors or pre-DOM gridCol XML generation before derived-output budgets. These independently reachable paths require controls before both import generation and layout; package byte/depth admission does not bound their semantic expansion.

severity.rationale: Public render/convert APIs accept untrusted documents and a tiny accepted input produces arbitrarily large generated XML. Impact is availability of the processing host; remote/shared exposure depends on the embedding application.
severity.changeConditions: Memory/CPU-limited isolated workers constrain impact; shared conversion service exposure increases affected availability.

rootCause.summary:
DOCX gridSpan and imported HTML colspan are trusted as output column cardinalities with only a lower bound. Both document-table paths lack a shared grid/output budget before generation and allocation.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The renderer accepts cell spans and row skips as unbounded machine integers and expands sparse semantic counts into dense vectors without checked cumulative arithmetic or an allocation budget. The sibling HTML importer lacks the same column budget and performs span-sized XML emission.

findings.remediation: Enforce practical per-cell span/row-skip and checked cumulative table/grid/output budgets across direct OOXML gridSpan/gridBefore/gridAfter and HTML/MHT colspan. Apply the common limit before HTML generation and before RawCell, column/preference/merge allocation or span-sized work; use checked sums and col+span arithmetic and return a typed conversion refusal. Neither importer-only nor later layout-only checking is sufficient. Use fallible allocation/reservation within those bounds so capacity failures become typed refusals.

counterEvidence: Archive inflation and XML input limits apply to original package bytes, which can remain tiny.
The parser defaults invalid/zero spans to one but valid huge positive spans remain unrestricted.
Process resource limits recommended by SECURITY.md constrain host impact without rejecting the expansion.
Package admission enforces byte, ZIP entry, XML depth and attribute limits before layout; those checks accept short decimal span attributes.
stretch_stale_spans returns early when used spans exceed existing columns (14172-14177); it does not cap spans.
SECURITY.md recommends process CPU/memory isolation; that mitigates host impact but does not prevent termination of a rendering worker.
limitations: No resource-exhaustion execution or observed service deployment.
No application code executed; no claim of a deployed remotely accessible renderer.
validation.method: Preserved already-validated Standard source evidence and assessments; serial semantic remediation-subsumption reduction only. No repository/dependency inspection, new validation, execution or attack-path analysis.
validation.summary:
Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing. Independently verified direct OOXML gridSpan parsing (14211-14215), column occupancy allocation (13601-13615), and merge vector resize (14637-14642); they share the missing bounded table cardinality control.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (already-validated offline Standard evidence; no reducer verification): Validated by reading the public PDF/render entry points (422-460,592-645), with_layout admission (769-799), table_block callers (8619,9178,17184,20598), span propagation (13200-13216,13466,13530-13536), allocation (13600-13619) and merge tracking (14600-14644). InputLimits fields (src/admission.rs:42-60) cover byte/entry/XML structural limits, not grid counts. Parent additionally validated HTML colspan parsing (altchunk.rs:562-566), sum (469-475) and 0..cols emission (489-490).
Assigned source also notes stretch_stale_spans returns early when used spans exceed existing columns (src/convert/mod.rs:14172-14177), leaving these numeric counts uncapped. gridSpan=1073741824 attempts a 4 GiB f32 column vector before other vectors, and the same positive HTML colspan emits over a billion gridCol elements; these are static consequences, not runtime measurements.

finding.title: Untrusted table spans cause unbounded renderer allocations
finding.summary: A small DOCX table can set w:gridSpan, w:gridBefore or w:gridAfter to a large usize. The shared PDF/PNG layout pipeline admits the package, derives column occupancy from these values, and allocates column and merge vectors at that size without a semantic budget. This can exhaust worker memory or panic before returning a normal conversion error. The HTML altChunk importer also accepts unbounded colspan and emits one gridCol per logical column.

severity.rationale: A document supplier can deterministically deny service to a process rendering the supplied file with very small input. Impact is availability of that process; no remote service or broader compromise is assumed, and process resource limits constrain host-wide impact.

confidence.rationale: Direct source trace from public conversion entry points through admission and uncapped attribute parsing to Vec allocation; no runtime exploit was executed.

codeEvidence.label: One XML element emitted per logical column
codeEvidence.explanation: end_table computes cols as maximum sum of cell.span (469-475) and emits unchecked attacker-sized output.

rootCause.summary: The renderer accepts cell spans and row skips as unbounded machine integers and expands sparse semantic counts into dense vectors without checked cumulative arithmetic or an allocation budget. The sibling HTML importer lacks the same column budget and performs span-sized XML emission.

finding.remediation: Apply a conservative semantic maximum to cell spans, row skips and cumulative grid columns before creating RawCell or allocating vectors. Use checked cumulative arithmetic and return a typed resource-limit error before any span-derived loop/allocation. Enforce the same budget in every shared layout path. Apply this semantic maximum during HTML colspan parsing and table emission as well.

counterEvidence: Package admission enforces byte, ZIP entry, XML depth and attribute limits before layout; those checks accept short decimal span attributes.
stretch_stale_spans returns early when used spans exceed existing columns (14172-14177); it does not cap spans.
SECURITY.md recommends process CPU/memory isolation; that mitigates host impact but does not prevent termination of a rendering worker.
limitations: No application code executed; no claim of a deployed remotely accessible renderer.

A tiny admitted document with gridSpan=1073741824 drives multi-GB allocation; usize::MAX causes capacity overflow panic. Entry/control context and sibling investigation pending.

previousFindings.title: Untrusted table spans cause unbounded renderer allocations
previousFindings.summary: A small DOCX table can set w:gridSpan, w:gridBefore or w:gridAfter to a large usize. The shared PDF/PNG layout pipeline admits the package, derives column occupancy from these values, and allocates column and merge vectors at that size without a semantic budget. This can exhaust worker memory or panic before returning a normal conversion error.

severity.rationale: A document supplier can deterministically deny service to a process rendering the supplied file with very small input. Impact is availability of that process; no remote service or broader compromise is assumed, and process resource limits constrain host-wide impact.

confidence.rationale: Direct source trace from public conversion entry points through admission and uncapped attribute parsing to Vec allocation; no runtime exploit was executed.

rootCause.summary: The renderer accepts cell spans and row skips as unbounded machine integers and expands sparse semantic counts into dense vectors without checked cumulative arithmetic or an allocation budget.

previousFindings.remediation: Apply a conservative semantic maximum to cell spans, row skips and cumulative grid columns before creating RawCell or allocating vectors. counterEvidence: Package admission enforces byte, ZIP entry, XML depth and attribute limits before layout; those checks accept short decimal span attributes.

previousFindings.title: Unbounded document table spans exhaust memory during rendering
previousFindings.summary: Untrusted DOCX table gridSpan and HTML/MHT altChunk colspan values become unrestricted output column counts. A tiny document can request a billion columns, causing layout-vector allocation or generated XML expansion before any output budget, exhausting memory and CPU despite package admission.

severity.rationale: Public render/convert APIs accept untrusted documents and a tiny accepted input produces arbitrarily large generated XML. Impact is availability of the processing host; remote/shared exposure depends on the embedding application.
severity.changeConditions: Memory/CPU-limited isolated workers constrain impact; shared conversion service exposure increases affected availability.

confidence.rationale: Source establishes package admission followed by HTML expansion, unrestricted colspan parsing, and direct count-driven XML generation; no destructive runtime proof was run.

codeEvidence.label: Rendering expands relationship-selected HTML
codeEvidence.explanation: Input admission precedes expansion, so its inflated input-byte budgets do not bound generated XML.

codeEvidence.label: OOXML span accepts huge positive values
codeEvidence.explanation: Raw DOCX tables can reach the same unrestricted numeric cardinality without an altChunk.

codeEvidence.label: Span totals directly size layout vectors
codeEvidence.explanation: A tiny gridSpan value represented by a short decimal string can trigger gigabytes of column allocation.

codeEvidence.label: Merge bookkeeping also grows with span
codeEvidence.explanation: The unbounded count also propagates into merge-state allocation and iteration.

rootCause.summary: DOCX gridSpan and imported HTML colspan are trusted as output column cardinalities with only a lower bound. Both document-table paths lack a shared grid/output budget before generation and allocation.

previousFindings.remediation: Enforce a common total table/grid budget for direct OOXML spans and HTML/MHT import before output generation or vector allocation. Reject excessive spans and use checked cumulative totals, returning a typed conversion refusal.

counterEvidence: Archive inflation and XML input limits apply to original package bytes, which can remain tiny.
The parser defaults invalid/zero spans to one but valid huge positive spans remain unrestricted.
Process resource limits recommended by SECURITY.md constrain host impact without rejecting the expansion.
limitations: No resource-exhaustion execution or observed service deployment.
validation.summary: Verified actual caller with_layout admits the package then expands internal altChunk bytes via html_to_wml; Builder accepts and stores the full span, and end_table emits cols grid elements before DOM parsing. Independently verified direct OOXML gridSpan parsing (14211-14215), column occupancy allocation (13601-13615), and merge vector resize (14637-14642); they share the missing bounded table cardinality control.

dataflow.summary: DOCX main document w:altChunk r:id -> relationship target part -> chunk_html -> html_to_wml -> Builder::start(td,colspan) -> end_table cols -> XML output loop. Ordinary OOXML path: w:gridSpan/@w:val -> cell_span -> RawCell.colspan -> occupancy -> cols allocation -> merge-state resize.

impact.summary: Processing-host memory exhaustion or prolonged CPU use.

likelihood.summary: The expansion is deterministic; exposure to untrusted callers depends on the embedding host.

reachability.summary: Public docx_to_png, render, report and PDF/layout paths call with_layout; attacker only needs to supply package bytes accepted by existing admission.
preconditions: A host renders/converts an attacker-controlled DOCX containing either a large w:gridSpan or an internal HTML/MHT chunk with a large colspan.

remediationTests: A tiny altChunk with colspan 1000000000 must fail before large output allocation.
Cover inclusive limits, cumulative spans across cells, integer overflow, nested tables, and both HTML and MHT import.
Cover direct OOXML gridSpan with tiny/no initial tblGrid, gridBefore/gridAfter variants, and merge bookkeeping as well as imported colspan.

findings.title: Repeated relationship IDs trigger quadratic repair work
findings.summary: Opening a package repairs identical duplicate relationship IDs. For n distinct IDs each repeated identically, each repair linearly searches an increasingly long Vec, producing quadratic CPU work on shallow metadata that fits existing byte and attribute limits.

severity.rationale: Attacker-controlled document data can exhaust CPU/memory or terminate its processing host through a public parser/conversion boundary. Shared or remote deployment is conditional; impact is availability.
severity.changeConditions: Isolated workers with process CPU/memory limits constrain impact; shared untrusted document services increase affected availability.

confidence.rationale: Parent independently inspected the cited source and actual caller/control path. Exploit inputs and resource exhaustion were not executed.

codeEvidence.explanation: Both root and part relationships are repaired; one relationship part can hold many records.

rootCause.summary:
Duplicate reporting uses repaired.contains on a growing Vec even though first-occurrence lookup already uses a HashMap. Root and every part relationship set invoke this repair. N distinct IDs each duplicated identically require N(N-1)/2 prior-ID string comparisons despite first-occurrence hashing; byte/depth/attribute checks do not limit this product.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): An ordered report vector is also used as a membership set, so the first duplicate of each new ID scans all preceding repaired IDs.

findings.remediation: Track already-reported duplicate IDs in a HashSet or alongside seen-map state, retaining a Vec only for deterministic reporting order. Optionally cap relationship-record/work totals before repair; test many distinct identical duplicate pairs while preserving deterministic repaired-ID order and conflicting-duplicate refusals.

counterEvidence: Conflicting duplicates are rejected before the linear repair search.
The 256-attribute cap is per element and does not cap the number of relationship records.
Actual inflated-byte budgets bound input bytes, but permit hundreds of thousands of shallow records.
Conflicting same-ID relationships fail closed.
Byte/inflation/XML budgets remain effective, but allow many small relationship elements.
External process CPU limits contain host impact.

rootCause.summary:
Each unrecognized ampersand restarts an unbounded delimiter search; the HTML ten-character filter is applied after scanning the full suffix.
oxml-opc 0.14.2 returns normalized Target attributes using quick-xml 0.41; PartFs::resolve_rel_target assumes raw attributes and calls unescape_xml_text again. Repeated & in valid XML thus becomes consecutive bare ampersands before the second decoder. Target existence checks occur after resolution. Around one million decoded ampersands from roughly five MB of encoded input imply about 500 billion character inspections, a static operation estimate rather than a benchmark.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: unescape_xml_text rescans the remaining input for every unresolved ampersand, and the relationship adapter redundantly invokes it on values already decoded by its current OPC parser.
Assigned discovery-0011 corroboration (preserved Standard assessment): The relationship consumer assumes raw attributes although its parser stores decoded values; its fallback entity scanner repeatedly scans the same suffix.

findings.remediation: Scan entities once without revisiting suffixes. In HTML, bound the search to the supported entity-length window before looking for ';'; give XML decoding a monotonic parser or bounded entity grammar. Remove PartFs's redundant relationship decoding when upstream supplies normalized attributes; retain the linear XML-helper repair for its other callers and the separate bounded HTML-helper repair. Preserve canonical literal '&' part names and one-time entity normalization through round trips.

findings.title: Pull-request code runs on shared self-hosted infrastructure
findings.summary: A lower-trust PR admitted to run can change a local action, build script, test or generator and execute it with self-hosted runner privileges. Four workflows share this missing isolation boundary; the local cache action documents private tokenless cache connectivity and reused checkout/disk.

severity.rationale: Runner-account code execution and private network access can compromise shared CI state. High potential impact has medium likelihood because GitHub PR approvals and external runner isolation are unknown. Confirmed disposable provisioning without shared authority would lower severity; automatic untrusted runs with trusted state would raise it.

confidence.rationale: Source establishes PR execution and shared cache/disk; actual runner lifecycle and external PR approval policy were not inspected.

codeEvidence.label: PR checkout executes on self-hosted
codeEvidence.code:
lint:
    name: fmt + clippy
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@89b12181fb390509a0842a86cc55eeb8eb928c1d # stable branch, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          components: rustfmt, clippy
          # jubarte-wasm is linted for the target it ships on.
          targets: wasm32-unknown-unknown
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      - run: cargo fmt --check
      - run: cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
codeEvidence.explanation: The checkout supplies the local action and Cargo/build inputs to a self-hosted runner.

codeEvidence.label: Self-hosted test leg
codeEvidence.code:
test:
    name: test (${{ matrix.os }})
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        os: [self-hosted, macos-latest, windows-latest]
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      # tests/corpus keeps the bench's file names, some past Windows'
      # 260-character path limit.
      - run: git config --global core.longpaths true
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@89b12181fb390509a0842a86cc55eeb8eb928c1d # stable branch, pinned 2026-10-01
      - if: matrix.os == 'self-hosted'
        uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      - if: matrix.os != 'self-hosted'
        uses: Swatinem/rust-cache@6323deb102c322ba6fcbdcafc7e3dddab59af2b6 # v2.9.2
      - uses: taiki-e/install-action@72f835688cb6c15903b796f704b01e652a2b8835 # cargo-llvm-cov tag, pinned 2026-10-01
        with:
          tool: cargo-nextest
      # Every failing test, not just the first binary's (the `ci` profile
      # does not fail fast), with JUnit XML for Codecov's test results.
      # The strict Markdown round trip is red until the reader work lands
      # (spec 2026-10-13 §5.4); md-roundtrip.yml is its gate, so this job
      # keeps reporting every other test.
      - run: cargo nextest run --all-features --profile ci -E 'not test(markdown_and_docx_round_trip_exactly)'

jobs:
  drift:
    name: generated docs drift
    runs-on: self-hosted
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - uses: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@89b12181fb390509a0842a86cc55eeb8eb928c1d # stable branch, pinned 2026-10-01
      - uses: ./.github/actions/mbx
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@c18668ad3cf93ea998bef934396af7bb5c839dc7 # v10.2.0
      # The generator runs jubarte-wasm/cli/bin/jubarte-redlines.mjs against

      - uses: actions/setup-node@949feb2413d6458794dcd2491c4babbbce0c15c1 # v7.1.0
        with:
          node-version: "24"
      - name: Regenerate and compare
        run: scripts/gen_docs.sh --check

codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk
codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.

rootCause.summary: PR-triggered jobs execute the PR checkout on shared self-hosted infrastructure without a source-enforced trusted-ref gate or disposable isolation. Token restrictions do not constrain arbitrary runner processes.

findings.remediation: Run lower-trust PR builds/tests/generators on GitHub-hosted or one-job disposable runners without trusted writable state or private infrastructure connectivity. Separate trusted main runners and enforce cache write authorization server-side. Apply consistently to ci, adoption, docs and md-roundtrip.

counterEvidence: contents:read and persist-credentials:false restrict GitHub token use, not runner process authority.
Fork PR approval is an external execution prerequisite.
Disposable runner configuration and server-side cache read/write enforcement are not available.
Release uses hosted runners; no direct release compromise is asserted.
limitations: Persistence/cache poisoning are conditional, not demonstrated.
Actual GitHub approvals and runner lifecycle remain unknown.
Final current-source check: every retained codeEvidence range exactly matched the live authorized checkout after its observed HEAD change; no historical revision was inspected.
validation.summary: Parent independently read all four workflows and the composite action, verified all PR triggers and affected runner/script selections, and confirmed documented shared resources. No live CI/cache probe was performed.

dataflow.summary: PR-owned checkout -> local action/Cargo/test/docs/example script -> self-hosted runner process -> runner filesystem/private network.
dataflow.outcome: arbitrary runner-account execution and private CI network reachability

impact.why: Potential trusted CI compromise from persistent state/private infrastructure access.

likelihood.why: PR admission and actual external isolation are unknown.

reachability.summary: A contributor submits a PR and any required platform approval allows the run. No repository write permission or privileged GitHub token is required after code executes.
preconditions: PR execution is allowed.
Configured self-hosted resources exist; external isolation determines persistence impact.

attackPath.summary: An allowed PR changes a local action, build script, test or generator; workflow checkout executes it on self-hosted and exposes runner-account resources.

remediationTests: Verify every PR-reachable job selects isolated runner infrastructure.
Verify PR runners cannot access trusted cache writes or retained trusted-job state.

codeEvidence.label: Shared private cache and reused disk
codeEvidence.code:
# The self-hosted runners share one mbx cache server on their private Docker
# network (`mbx-cache`), so a crate one runner compiled is a cache hit on the
# others. The server takes no token: mbx sends none over plain HTTP, and only
# the runners can reach it. mbx publishes only from pushes to a protected
# branch; pull requests read. GitHub-hosted runners cannot reach the server,
# so jobs that also run there keep Swatinem/rust-cache on those legs.
runs:
  using: composite
  steps:
    - uses: jdx/mr-boxington-action@47ce49b32025d93a7a2f4570815afaa2b7092240 # v1.7.2
      with:
        backend: remote
        version: "1.24.1"
        remote-url: http://mbx-cache:7543
        namespace: jandira-tech/jubarte-redlines
        # Linked test binaries are the largest outputs by far: with
        # them cached, one test job left an 84 GiB store and a 79 GiB target
        # on 2026-10-17, and uploads drained at 1 MB/s. Cache compilations only.
        cache-links: "false"
    # Every job on a runner builds in the same checkout, so mbx always counts
    # that checkout's managed target as the most recently used and never
    # collects it: on 2026-10-17 three of them reached 69-220 GiB in a few
    # hours and filled the disk the four runners share. Each job now starts
    # from an empty target, restored from the store and the cache server,
    # and each runner's store keeps to a fixed share of the disk.
codeEvidence.explanation: The cache is tokenless and reachable from runners, shares main namespace, and comments describe shared checkouts/disk. Server enforcement is unavailable.

findings.title: Converting legacy DOC text with a long numeric prefix causes quadratic work
findings.summary: For each period or closing parenthesis, the Markdown escaper rescans the full preceding text. A long digit prefix followed by many periods repeatedly scans the same digits, consuming disproportionate CPU on a small legacy DOC.

severity.rationale: High availability impact with medium likelihood: a victim must import the supplied legacy DOC and lacks sufficient per-job CPU/memory isolation.
severity.changeConditions: Lower with effective process CPU/memory limits; automated shared imports increase likelihood.

confidence.rationale: Independent static trace establishes attacker-controlled legacy text/table structure and disproportionate conversion work. No runtime benchmark was performed.

codeEvidence.label: Converting legacy DOC text with a long numeric prefix causes quadratic work
codeEvidence.explanation: Public doc_to_markdown/doc_to_docx convert parsed spans/cells with escape_line. The outer character loop recomputes whether the entire prefix is ASCII digits at every '.' or ')'. Once one period follows a long numeric prefix, each later period still scans all preceding digits before short-circuiting on that first period, making work quadratic.

codeEvidence.label: Public legacy conversion invokes unbudgeted serialization
codeEvidence.explanation: Both direct conversion APIs expose the legacy document serialization path, and CLI convert invokes doc_to_docx on OLE input.

rootCause.summary: Public doc_to_markdown/doc_to_docx convert parsed spans/cells with escape_line. The outer character loop recomputes whether the entire prefix is ASCII digits at every '.' or ')'. Once one period follows a long numeric prefix, each later period still scans all preceding digits before short-circuiting on that first period, making work quadratic.

findings.remediation: Track a running all-ASCII-digits prefix flag while iterating once, or identify the sole initial numeric-list delimiter once. Preserve escaping behavior with linear work.

counterEvidence: Physical CFB streams and numeric offsets remain bounded; they do not bound this generated work.

limitations: No crafted DOC, application execution or peak-resource measurement.

findings.title: Listing many comments over one large range multiplies retained anchor text
findings.summary: A document with many comments covering the same large text range is small relative to the comment listing it produces. list_comments copies the full range into every CommentRecord without an expanded-output budget, allowing a compact document to demand gigabytes of retained memory.

severity.rationale: High availability impact with medium likelihood because document content alone controls comment count and overlapping range size; a victim must request comment listing or a consumer that lists them.
severity.changeConditions: Effective host isolation and narrower exposure lower impact/likelihood; automatic untrusted workflows increase exposure.

confidence.rationale: Source-backed input-to-operation trace and explicit controls/counterevidence; no application execution or deployment assumption.

codeEvidence.label: Public comment listing materializes records
codeEvidence.explanation: Caller-controlled comments are collected into a single Vec and filled one by one.

codeEvidence.label: Each comment clones its full anchored range
codeEvidence.explanation: The same source text can be copied into thousands of independent records without aggregate bounds.

rootCause.summary: comments_in materializes all comment records into a Vec and calls Anchors::fill for each one. fill clones the entire anchored paragraph or joined range into each record independently. Shared source text is therefore retained once per comment, with no aggregate anchor/output limit.

findings.remediation: Enforce a cumulative comment-anchor/output byte budget before cloning, return a typed refusal or bounded/truncated representation, and consider shared ranges or streaming records instead of duplicating every full anchor in memory.

counterEvidence: Repeating anchored text is useful intended output behavior, but its aggregate allocation is not budgeted.
Admission byte/depth limits still apply to input.
No runtime peak memory was measured and external process limits can contain impact.
limitations: No crafted file or application execution.
validation.summary: Independently traced public list_comments132-134, comments_in145-156 and Anchors::fill352-398. Package byte/depth budgets do not cap that output product.

findings.title: Python and Node plan recording can overwrite unrelated files through staging symlinks
findings.summary: The Python and Node CLIs write plans through a predictable .<plan>.<PID>.partial pathname using nonexclusive truncating writes. A local actor who can create entries in the plan directory can preplace a symlink there and make the victim overwrite another file it can write, before the intended plan replacement.

severity.rationale: Potentially high file-integrity impact but low likelihood: requires a malicious local actor sharing write access to the selected plan directory, knowledge/prediction of the victim PID and writable target under victim authority. No remote exploit or RCE is established.
severity.changeConditions: Raise if plans routinely live in cross-user writable workspaces or a privileged automation service records plans there; private per-user directories substantially reduce exposure.

confidence.rationale: Both adapter source operations and caller guards inspected; neither exclusively creates staging. Standard Path.write_bytes/fs.writeFileSync following/truncation semantics establish the overwrite. No filesystem reproduction.

rootCause.summary:
Both recorders derive a staging filename from final plan basename and process ID, then use an ordinary write before atomic rename/replace. No exclusive create or private staging directory binds that name to a newly owned file. An existing symlink is therefore followed during the write, even though the eventual rename is atomic for the plan target.
Assigned discovery-0012 corroboration: Plan recording independently reimplements filesystem publication in Python and Node with PID-only temporary names and nonexclusive truncation, bypassing the native recorder's private staging controls.

findings.remediation: Use exclusive, unpredictable staging owned by a private directory, hold the opened handle through writing, and rename that verified file. Reuse the native publication design or equivalent mkstemp/exclusive wx APIs and never follow existing staging entries.

counterEvidence: Requires write access to the parent plan directory and victim target permissions.
Private plan directories and dry-run avoid the path.
Native Rust publication uses private exclusive UUID staging and does not share this specific defect.
Dry-run and failed preview skip publication.
Exploitation requires another user's writable-directory authority; default private directories are not assumed exposed.
Native Rust recorder uses hardened publish_paths and is not affected by these adapter staging writes.
limitations: No attack was executed.
Exact PID discovery and shared-directory permissions are deployment prerequisites.
No symlinks were created and application code was not run.

findings.title: Legacy edit-anchor searches compare long prefixes at every character
findings.summary: Legacy plan resolution searches for an anchor with starts_with at every character position, including its normalized fallback. A repetitive paragraph paired with a long near-matching anchor can force quadratic CPU work before the plan is refused or applied.

severity.rationale: Potential high CPU impact but low likelihood: requires a consumer to resolve a long attacker-influenced legacy plan anchor against a repetitive document. No remote/automatic hostile-plan deployment established.
severity.changeConditions: Effective host isolation and narrower exposure lower impact/likelihood; automatic untrusted workflows increase exposure.

confidence.rationale: Source-backed input-to-operation trace and explicit controls/counterevidence; no application execution or deployment assumption.

codeEvidence.label: Legacy find_range forwards caller anchors
codeEvidence.explanation: Normal plan range resolution reaches locate with the caller's find text.

codeEvidence.label: Exact search compares an anchor at every character
codeEvidence.explanation: Every suffix can repeat the same long prefix comparison.

codeEvidence.label: Normalized fallback repeats the same search
codeEvidence.explanation: Normalization changes representation but does not remove the quadratic search behavior.

rootCause.summary: locate builds hits_of by applying starts_with(needle) to each text suffix. reading_hits repeats the same algorithm after normalization. Long shared prefixes are compared repeatedly with no search-work budget, unlike the KMP-based v2 candidate matcher. An a^N paragraph and a^(N/2)b anchor make each early comparison traverse most of the anchor before failing.

findings.remediation: Use a linear-time substring matcher for exact and normalized legacy anchors, reusing the v2 KMP approach, while preserving overlapping-hit semantics and source-offset mapping. Add explicit cumulative matching-work limits where needed.

counterEvidence: v2 candidate matching uses a linear KMP implementation; this report is limited to the legacy resolver.
Short anchors/ordinary paragraphs are bounded in practice.
Caller-controlled plan text is an additional prerequisite, not automatically supplied by every malicious document.
limitations: No crafted file or application execution.
validation.summary: Independently followed Replace -> find_range4164-4180 -> locate5763-5820 and the normalized fallback79-92. Both search implementations inspect every character suffix; no anchor-length/product-work cap appears in this path. The concrete high-cost case needs influence over both document text and the selected legacy anchor, so likelihood is lower than document-only parser findings.

findings.title: Streaming XML hash repeatedly rescans growing escaped opening tags
findings.summary: HashXmlBuf searches the entire accumulated opening tag for > after every emitted fragment. Escaped attribute values emit one fragment per character; retained custom-namespace paragraph attributes select this fallback hashing path, causing quadratic CPU consumption within admitted XML sizes.

severity.rationale: A supplied document directly induces disproportionate memory/CPU consumption in a victim processing it. Impact is process availability; no remote-service or cross-tenant deployment is inferred.

confidence.rationale: Direct offline source validation establishes caller-controlled input, effective controls and sensitive operation. No triggering input or application code executed.

codeEvidence.label: Every fragment rescans the growing root tag
codeEvidence.explanation: A large escaped attribute is emitted in tiny fragments before any > appears.

codeEvidence.label: Attribute escaping emits one fragment per character
codeEvidence.code:
for c in s.chars() {
        match c {
            '&' => out.push_str("&"),
            '<' => out.push_str("<"),
            '>' => out.push_str(">"),
            '"' => out.push_str("""),
            '\t' => out.push_str("	"),
            '\n' => out.push_str("
"),
            '\r' => out.push_str(""),
            _ => out.push(c),
        }
codeEvidence.explanation: Each escaped ampersand appends five bytes then triggers another whole-tag scan.

codeEvidence.label: Custom namespace selects fallback hashing
codeEvidence.explanation: Retained attributes outside Word/empty namespace cause fast hash to decline.

rootCause.summary: Root-tag buffering repeatedly searches old bytes on every character-sized escaped fragment instead of searching newly appended bytes or signaling tag completion.

findings.remediation: Search only the new fragment for the root-tag terminator or expose explicit tag-completion state from serialization. Preserve linear behavior for escaped values and test large retained custom attributes through public comparison.

counterEvidence: Simple paragraphs fast-hash; custom namespace causes explicit fallback.
One namespace declaration and one permitted attribute stay within count/name/value/start-tag budgets.
SHA1 content keys' nonauthentication role is unrelated to this CPU issue.
Identical input packages shortcut comparison; differing documents reach normal hashing.
limitations: No runtime reproduction or deployment verified.
validation.summary: Parent verified HashXmlBuf append/find (serialize.rs:501-516), character escaping (548-558), retained paragraph attrs (preprocess.rs:306-312), custom-namespace fallback (742-769), block_sha1_from_source fallback (657-679) and comparison block-hash pipeline (comparer/mod.rs:655-667; preprocess.rs:1276-1281).
